cards.title: P versus BPP
cards.formal: Does \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{BPP}\)? Precisely, for every language L for which a randomized Turing machine R runs in polynomial time on every input and every random tape, and satisfies $\Pr[R(x)=1_L(x)]\ge2/3$ for every binary string x, does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine deciding L correctly on every x? The polynomial time bound of the deterministic machine may depend on R.
cards.definitions: Input length is \(n=|x|\). A polynomial-time bound means \(C(n+1)^{k}\) steps for fixed constants C,k, independent of x and of the random bits. R uses independent unbiased random bits, at most one fresh bit per computation step, and outputs a single bit. Its error may be on either yes or no inputs, but is bounded separately on each input. P consists of deterministic polynomial-time decision languages and BPP of languages meeting the randomized guarantee above. These are total decision problems, with no excluded promise inputs. No advice, oracle, quantum operations, or input distribution is allowed. The requested deterministic simulation may use a different algorithm; it need not reproduce R's random choices, preserve its precise exponent, or be generated by an effective compiler from R.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This determines whether random bits add power to efficient total decision computation. It is a central organizing question for pseudorandom generators, explicit constructions, and the connection between circuit lower bounds and algorithm design.

importance.reason: The main general derandomization question for polynomial-time decision algorithms, with broad consequences for the role of randomness and for hardness-versus-randomness techniques.

progress.text: Adleman establishes \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq \mathrm{P}\)/poly. Suitable fixed random advice exists for each input length, but uniform polynomial-time computation of that advice is not supplied.

Impagliazzo and Wigderson prove \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{BPP}\) if there is a Boolean function computable in time \(2^{O(n)}\) that requires circuits of size \(2^{c n}\), for some \(c>0\) and all sufficiently large n. The circuit-hardness assumption remains essential to this theorem.

Doron, Moshkovitz, Oh, and Zuckerman improve conditional pseudorandomness parameters for algorithms satisfying an insensitivity property of their correct and incorrect random tapes. This concerns finer generators for a specified algorithm class, not unconditional removal of randomness from all BPP computations.

Version 9 of a preprint by Tianrong Lin claims the opposite conclusion \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{BPP}\), along with stronger separations. This review has not verified that construction or located independent primary validation. The claimed separation is recorded without treating it as established.

context_blocks.text: Randomized decision algorithms may use randomness to avoid exceptional choices or to test a property through a small sample. Their guarantee is pointwise: even the worst input must receive the correct answer with high probability. Repeating an algorithm reduces its error but leaves it randomized. The question asks whether every such use of randomness can ultimately be replaced by a deterministic polynomial computation.

Exhaustive majority evaluation over all random tapes has a time cost exponential in their length. That is correct, but takes exponential time when the tape has polynomial length. A suitable pseudorandom generator would reduce the search to a polynomial-size set of tapes, constructed efficiently. The hard part is ensuring that this small set fools the computation on every input.

A nonuniform version of this idea already works: after error amplification, an averaging argument supplies one polynomial-length advice string that works for every input of a given length. This proves BPP is contained in P/poly. The string can depend on the input length without an efficient procedure to find it, which is exactly why that inclusion does not answer the uniform question.

Strong circuit hardness provides a conditional route to full derandomization. Impagliazzo and Wigderson show that an exponentially circuit-hard function computable in exponential time suffices. The condition is substantially more specific than merely \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). Current work also studies the amount of slowdown and the structure of the randomized algorithm, producing finer conditional results without an unconditional equality proof.

This card concerns computing one correct decision bit. Sampling a distribution, producing one of many valid witnesses, or deciding only inputs with a promise leads to related but different formulations. Keeping these tasks separate prevents a derandomization theorem for one setting from being silently substituted for another.

cards.title: Optimal explicit pseudorandom generators for read-once branching programs
cards.formal: Do there exist absolute constants C,D and a uniform family of generators \(G_{n,w,p}:\{0,1\}^{s}\to \{0,1\}^{n}\), for all integers \(n,w\ge 2\) and \(p\ge 1\), with \(s\le C(\log _{2} n+\log _{2} w+p)\), such that \(\left|\Pr_{u\text{ uniform in }\{0,1\}^{s}}[B(G_{n,w,p}(u))=1]-\Pr_{z\text{ uniform in }\{0,1\}^{n}}[B(z)=1]\right|\le2^{-p}\) for every length-n, width-at-most-w ordered read-once branching program B? Require a single deterministic algorithm that, given n,w,p,u and an output position i, computes \(G_{n,w,p}(u)_{i}\) using at most \(D(\log _{2} n+\log _{2} w+p)\) work bits and time \((nw\cdot 2^{p})^{D}\).
cards.definitions: An ordered read-once branching program has layers \(V_{0},\ldots ,V_{n}\), each containing at most w states, a designated initial state in \(V_{0}\), and an accepting subset of \(V_{n}\). For each layer \(i- 1\), each state has one outgoing edge labeled 0 and one labeled 1 to \(V_{i}\). On input z, the program follows the edge labeled \(z_{i}\) at step i and accepts exactly when the final state is accepting. Different edges may merge; neither regularity nor permutation transitions are required. The order is the fixed order \(z_{1},\ldots ,z_{n}\). Programs may be arbitrary nonuniform objects, but the generator cannot inspect their descriptions. The parameters and seed are read-only inputs to the generator algorithm, and the output bit is written separately; all work space, counters and intermediate storage are counted. Seed length is a computable function of the parameters within the stated resources. Uniform seeds induce an ordinary probability distribution, without signed or externally assigned weights. Set \(\varepsilon =2^{- p}\); this dyadic formulation gives the usual \(O(\log (nw/\varepsilon ))\) target for arbitrary positive error by rounding down to a smaller dyadic tolerance.

cards.why: An optimal generator would remove randomness from logarithmic-space computation and identify how little entropy suffices to fool every small-memory streaming computation. cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. ECCC TR26-064 revision 3 explicitly retains the optimal general PRG target and the log-squared barrier. Its new generator is weighted; the July TR26-123 result is restricted to permutation programs. This card requires one ordinary, program-independent distribution family and optimal seed length as well as optimal work space.

context_blocks.text: The program processes a long stream while remembering only its current state. Width w corresponds to about \(\log _{2} w\) bits of memory; length n is the number of random bits it can inspect. A pseudorandom generator replaces that long random stream with the deterministic expansion of a much shorter genuinely random seed. The requirement is simultaneous: the same generated distribution must fool every permitted program, even though their transition tables may be entirely different.

There is no information-theoretic obstacle to the seed-length target. After padding to w states, the number of programs is at most \(w\cdot 2^{w}\cdot w^{2nw}\). Choose a list of independent uniform n-bit strings and use a uniformly chosen list position as the seed. A concentration bound and union bound show that a list of \(O(\varepsilon ^{- 2}(nw \log  w+w))\) strings suffices to approximate every acceptance probability. Indexing that list takes \(O(\log  n+\log  w+\log (1/\varepsilon ))\) bits. The argument does not tell us how to generate its entries in the tiny workspace required here.

The computational payoff is direct. Fix an input to a bounded-error logarithmic-space randomized machine and view its evolution on random bits as a polynomial-length, polynomial-width branching program. A logarithmic seed permits enumeration of all seeds, regeneration of individual pseudorandom bits and counting accepting runs within logarithmic space. With constant error small enough to preserve the acceptance gap, this would prove \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{BPL}\). The card asks for a uniform generator, which is a particular strong route to that complexity-class equality.

Nisan’s construction gives seed length \(O(\log  n\cdot \log (nw/\varepsilon ))\). For polynomial width and constant error this is \(O(\log ^{2}n)\), so reaching the target would remove an entire logarithmic factor. The difficulty is generating a universally useful sample space in little space, rather than merely showing that some sample space exists. Even considerable improvements for simpler transition structures need not survive arbitrary merging of states.

Weighted pseudorandom generators relax the distribution requirement. They approximate acceptance by a weighted sum of program evaluations, with weights that may be negative. Hoza’s RANDOM 2021 construction attains seed length \(O(\log ^{2}n+\log (1/\varepsilon ))\) for width-n, length-n programs, improving the dependence on small error. Such weighted estimates can support deterministic simulation, but negative mass cannot be sampled as an ordinary probability distribution over the generated strings.

Cheng and Wu’s SODA 2026 work improves weighted generators across width and error regimes. Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma’s May 2026 revision improves error reduction and the dependence on the input alphabet. It still constructs a weighted object. Its discussion credits Cheng and Hoza’s earlier reduction showing that sufficiently good ordinary-generator dependence on alphabet size and error would break the log-squared barrier. That implication does not turn the newly constructed weighted generator into an ordinary one.

The role of hitting sets provides another useful distinction. A hitting set ensures that an accepting string is included when the accepting fraction is sufficiently large; it does not directly approximate that fraction. Cheng and Hoza prove that sufficiently strong logspace hitting sets nevertheless imply two-sided logspace derandomization through a more involved reduction. Their results explain why a derandomization theorem need not arrive packaged as the universal probability distribution requested here.

Cohen, Doron and Goldgraber’s July 2026 paper gives an ordinary generator for permutation programs with seed \(O((\log  w+\log (1/\varepsilon ))\log  n)\), by a new analysis of the INW generator. In this subclass each symbol acts bijectively on the states between layers. The result has optimal logarithmic dependence on length when width and error are fixed, but the permutation promise excludes the arbitrary state merging allowed in this card.

cards.title: L versus BPL
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{BPL}\)? Equivalently, for every language \(S\subseteq \{0,1\}\)* decided with two-sided error at most \(1/3\) by a uniform randomized Turing machine using \(O(\log (n+2))\) work space and polynomial time on inputs of length n, is there a uniform deterministic Turing machine deciding S with \(O(\log (n+2))\) work space?
cards.definitions: The machines have a finite description, a read-only two-way input tape, and a fixed finite number of work tapes over a fixed finite alphabet. Space counts all visited work-tape cells; the input tape is excluded. A randomized machine receives independent fair coin outcomes one at a time, without a freely rereadable random tape: an outcome must be stored in counted work space to be remembered. It halts with ACCEPT or REJECT on every input and every random tape within \(K(n+2)^{c}\) steps and uses at most \(K \log _{2}(n+2)\) work cells, for some constants K,c depending only on the machine. For each input x, acceptance probability is at least \(2/3\) if \(x\in S\) and at most \(1/3\) if \(x\notin S\). This is a language problem with no promise excluding intermediate-probability inputs. A deterministic decider must halt and give the correct answer on every input; any halting deterministic logarithmic-space decider has polynomially many configurations and hence polynomial running time. Both classes are uniform and have no advice. The deterministic machine and its space constant may depend on S. The equality does not demand a computable compiler transforming arbitrary machine descriptions, nor a particular pseudorandom-generator construction.

context_blocks.text: A logarithmic-space computation can maintain indices and counters while remembering only a small part of the input. Randomness lets it explore many possible choices without storing all of them. The equality asks whether this apparent extra power disappears when the required output is only a bounded-error decision about the input.

The memory convention is central. Fresh random outcomes can be read once; a machine cannot revisit an arbitrarily long random string without paying for its storage or reconstructing it. Conversely, the deterministic simulator is allowed a different constant in its logarithmic-space bound. The question concerns equality of language classes, not identical execution traces.

Saks and Zhou gave a deterministic simulation using \(O(\log ^{3/2} n)\) space. Hoza improved the bound to \(O(\log ^{3/2} n / \sqrt{\log  \log  n})\), with the expression understood asymptotically. These bounds are substantially below squared logarithmic space but remain above a constant multiple of log n.

The 2026 work of Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma improves error reduction for weighted pseudorandom generators. Its revised account distinguishes weighted generators from ordinary generators and attributes the relevant arity/error connection to Cheng and Hoza. Those parameter improvements do not establish the equality of classes asked here.

The catalogue separately contains a concrete optimal-generator problem for read-once branching programs. Such a construction can have consequences for logarithmic-space derandomization, but the language-class equality does not prescribe that particular construction. This completed card retains the original TCS-0026 identity and Wigderson reference while making the computation and error models explicit.

cards.title: Optimal deterministic restricted-isometry matrices
cards.formal: Do there exist universal constants \(C,B,b>0\) and a deterministic algorithm which, for every pair of integers \(N\ge 2\) and \(2\le s\le N\), outputs in at most \(B N^{b}\) bit operations a rational \(m\times N\) matrix A, with \(m\le C s \ln (eN/s)\), such that \((2/3)\Vert x\Vert _{2}^{2}\le \Vert Ax\Vert _{2}^{2}\le (4/3)\Vert x\Vert _{2}^{2}\) for every real vector \(x\in \mathbb{R} ^{N}\) with at most s nonzero coordinates?
cards.definitions: The input consists of N and s in binary. The output is an explicit list of all entries of A, each encoded as a signed integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary. Its total encoding length must also be at most \(B N^{b}\). Time is ordinary deterministic Turing-machine bit complexity, polynomial in N; randomness, advice and unit-cost exact real arithmetic are unavailable. The row count m is a positive integer chosen by the algorithm. The same constants and algorithm work for all allowed pairs N,s. The norm is Euclidean, and the displayed inequalities concern squared norms. They define restricted isometry of order s and distortion \(\delta =1/3\). context_blocks.text: Suppose an unknown vector has N coordinates but only s of them matter. A measurement matrix replaces the vector by m linear measurements. Sparsity allows m to be much smaller than N, but the matrix must preserve every possible sparse direction if the measuring device is to work uniformly. The question asks whether a short, guaranteed measurement design can be computed without random choices.

The restricted-isometry requirement has a concrete spectral interpretation. For every set S of at most s column indices, all eigenvalues of \(A_{S}^{T}A_{S}\) must lie between \(2/3\) and \(4/3\). Thus columns must behave almost orthogonally in every small group. Checking only individual column lengths, only pairs of columns, or a large collection of sampled test vectors leaves many of these simultaneous constraints untested.

This condition supports stable sparse recovery. If a matrix has restricted isometry of order 2t with distortion \(1/3\), then two different t-sparse signals cannot have identical measurements: their difference has at most 2t nonzero coordinates. Standard recovery theorems also give robust reconstruction by \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) minimization. The distinction between order t and order 2t is necessary; injectivity for t-sparse differences alone would not compare arbitrary t-sparse signals.

Random independent Bernoulli or Gaussian matrices attain \(m=O(s \log (eN/s))\) for fixed distortion, and matching row lower bounds make this the optimal order for \(s\ge 2\). Rao’s paper summarizes this benchmark and improves the amount of randomness needed to attain it. The unresolved resource in the card is therefore deterministic construction time, rather than whether matrices with the desired geometric property exist.

Requiring rational output does not destroy the random benchmark. For example, choose the number of rows to be a perfect square \(t^{2}\) within a constant factor of a sufficiently large target value, and use independent entries ±\(1/t\). This keeps the usual normalized Bernoulli construction while giving an exact, short binary description of every entry. The real difficulty is choosing all the signs deterministically with a proof that every sparse direction is preserved.

One basic deterministic analysis bounds the coherence \(\mu\), the largest absolute inner product between two unit columns. Gershgorin’s theorem then gives restricted-isometry constant at most \((s- 1)\mu\). When \(\mu\) is about \(1/\sqrt{m}\), this argument certifies only s on the order of \(\sqrt{m}\). This is a limitation of that sufficient-condition analysis, commonly called the square-root bottleneck, rather than an impossibility theorem for deterministic matrices.

Bourgain, Dilworth, Ford, Konyagin and Kutzarova broke that bottleneck in a restricted parameter regime. Their explicit construction uses additive-combinatorial and exponential-sum estimates to control interactions beyond pairwise coherence. It is a major proof that deterministic analysis can go further, but its small exponent improvement does not reach the optimal \(s \log (eN/s)\) row count uniformly in N and s.

Rao’s construction achieves the optimal row order with \(O(s \log (N/s) \log  s)\) random bits in the sparse parameter regime discussed in the paper. Its proof extends the Hanson–Wright inequality to biased distributions. Reducing the seed length makes progress toward explicit construction, but enumerating all seeds can still take far more than polynomial time, and recognizing a successful seed is a separate issue.

The inherited 2025 paper of Fickus and Lake studies highly symmetric equiangular tight frames, which minimize coherence. It analyzes their minimal dependent column sets through regular simplices and designs. Such structure is informative in both directions: a dependent set of r columns immediately prevents restricted isometry of order r with distortion less than one. Optimal pairwise geometry alone does not guarantee the higher-order property.

For a simple illustration, the \(m+1\) unit vertices of a regular simplex in \(\mathbb{R} ^{m}\) have small and equal pairwise inner products, yet their sum is zero. Their coefficient vector of all ones is therefore a nonzero sparse kernel vector. The example explains why an attractive frame construction must be accompanied by control over all relevant column subsets, not just a calculation of coherence.

The all-parameter formulation also matters. The identity matrix handles s comparable to N, while many explicit algebraic constructions work only along particular dimension sequences or for specified sparsity ranges. A resolution must cover the intermediate sparse regimes with one polynomial-time procedure. Likewise, statistical recovery guarantees and \(\ell\)\(_{1}\)-norm versions of restricted isometry answer different geometric questions.

cards.title: Unconditional subexponential simulation of BPP
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{SUBEXP}\) unconditionally? Here the subexponential class is the intersection
\[\mathrm{SUBEXP}=\bigcap_{k\ge1}\mathrm{DTIME}\!\left(2^{n^{1/k}}\right).\]
Thus, for every language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) decidable with two-sided bounded error in randomized polynomial time, and for every integer \(k\ge1\), must there exist a deterministic algorithm deciding \(L\) on every input in time \(O(2^{n^{1/k}})\)? The algorithm and the constant in its time bound may depend on \(L,k\). The target selects the subexponential question in the source's Open Problem 3.4; its separate quasipolynomial-time question is stronger.
cards.why: This asks whether randomness can provide a much larger speedup than the usual derandomization conjectures predict, even after allowing deterministic time far beyond polynomial. An unconditional simulation would move the general worst-case upper bound into the source’s much smaller subexponential class. A counterexample would establish a major separation between randomized and deterministic computation.

cards.definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings. An algorithm decides \(L\) if it halts and outputs one exactly on inputs in \(L\), and zero on all other inputs. Use uniform multitape Turing machines with finite descriptions independent of input length. One transition costs one time unit. A randomized machine may additionally request independent unbiased bits, at unit cost per bit. It has no advice, oracle or preprocessing that depends on input length without being computed by the machine.

Membership in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) means that there are such a randomized machine \(M\) and constants \(a,C\ge1\) with worst-case runtime at most \(C(n+1)^a\) on every length-\(n\) input and every random tape, and with
\[x\in L\Rightarrow\Pr[M(x)=1]\ge2/3,\qquad x\notin L\Rightarrow\Pr[M(x)=1]\le1/3.\]
This is a class of total decision problems. The acceptance-probability gap holds on every input; it is not a promise that an external user must supply.

The notation \(L\in\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^{1/k}})\) means that a deterministic machine decides \(L\) and has worst-case runtime at most \(C_k\lceil2^{n^{1/k}}\rceil\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), for some fixed \(C_k\). All finitely many smaller inputs must also be decided correctly and with termination. Requiring every integer \(k\) is equivalent to requiring time \(O(2^{n^\varepsilon})\) for every fixed real \(\varepsilon>0\). The machine is allowed to change with the exponent; an effective compiler taking \(M,k\) and producing the simulator is not an additional requirement.

This definition of SUBEXP is the source's intersection of subpower-exponential time classes. A single \(2^{o(n)}\)-time bound, such as \(2^{n/\log n}\), need not meet it. Likewise, correctness only on most inputs, or on infinitely many input lengths, is insufficient. The simulator must decide the same language exactly on all strings.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the inclusion or its negation. A positive proof must cover every BPP language and every fixed exponent \(1/k\), without a hardness assumption, oracle or advice. A negative proof must establish a language in BPP that is outside one of the deterministic time classes in the displayed intersection. A conditional simulation, a simulation for a particular randomized problem, or a heuristic correct on almost all inputs does not settle the question.

context_blocks.text: Enumerating every random tape gives a deterministic simulation in \(2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\) time. A polynomial-time randomized algorithm can use polynomially many random bits, so this direct simulation gives EXP rather than the displayed SUBEXP target.
If \(\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm P\), the desired inclusion follows. The converse is not asserted: a subexponential simulator may still take much more than polynomial time.

Known hardness-versus-randomness theorems yield much stronger derandomization under suitable circuit lower-bound assumptions. For example, the Impagliazzo–Wigderson theorem derives BPP = P from exponential circuit hardness for a language computable in single-exponential time. Those hardness hypotheses are part of the conditional theorem and cannot be removed by citing it.

Fixing a good random tape separately for each length gives a nonuniform object. Uniformity requires a finite deterministic algorithm that computes its behavior; a sequence of good tapes supplied for free does not meet the target.

cards.title: Linear-seed hardness-to-randomness sampling
cards.formal:
Does there exist one explicit family of point samplers
\[H_{\ell,s}:\{0,1\}^{d(\ell,s)}\to(\{0,1\}^{\ell})^{m(\ell,s)}\]
and absolute constants \(C\ge1\) and rational \(\beta\in(0,1)\) with the following property for every pair of integers \(\ell\ge1\), \(s\ge2\)? The lengths obey
\[d(\ell,s)\le C\ell,\qquad \max\{1,\lfloor s^{\beta}\rfloor\}\le m(\ell,s)\le s.\]
For every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^{\ell}\to\{0,1\}\) satisfying
\[\forall B\text{ of size at most }s,\quad\Pr_{x\sim U_{\ell}}[B(x)=f(x)]\le\tfrac12+\tfrac1s,\]
form the \(m\)-bit generator
\[G_f(z)=f(H_{\ell,s}(z)_1)\,f(H_{\ell,s}(z)_2)\cdots f(H_{\ell,s}(z)_m).\]
Must it then satisfy
\[\forall D\text{ of size at most }m,\quad\bigl|\Pr_{z\sim U_d}[D(G_f(z))=1]-\Pr_{u\sim U_m}[D(u)=1]\bigr|\le1/m?\]
The circuits, explicitness and probability spaces are defined below. The sampler is chosen independently of \(f\); each output bit of \(G_f\) is exactly one evaluation of \(f\) at the corresponding sampled point.
cards.why: This asks whether strong average-case hardness can be converted into many pseudorandom bits while using a seed only a constant factor longer than one input to the hard function, and preserving an especially simple evaluation form. Such a result would make the hardness-to-randomness connection more modular and usable across different computational classes. The restriction concerns the structure of the transformation, not merely the final existence of a short-seed generator.

cards.definitions:
\(U_t\) denotes the uniform distribution on \(t\)-bit strings. The probabilities in the premise and conclusion use fresh independent uniform strings of the indicated lengths. They are computational distinguishability guarantees, not statistical closeness against unbounded tests.

A Boolean circuit is a finite acyclic graph with input wires, free Boolean constants, fan-in-two AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, and one output wire. Size counts computation gates, including NOT gates, but not input wires or constants. The circuits \(B\) and \(D\) are deterministic and completely nonuniform; \(B\) has \(\ell\) inputs and \(D\) has \(m\). Their choices may depend on all parameters and on \(f\). They have no oracle access to \(f\). Allowing additional independent random input wires does not change these guarantees, because fixing the random bits gives a deterministic circuit of no greater size and averaging preserves the displayed inequalities. The premise means that even the best size-\(s\) predictor has advantage at most \(1/s\) over a fair guess.

Explicitness is uniform deterministic polynomial-time computation of the sampler. There are fixed multitape Turing machines and integers \(K,q\ge1\) such that the parameter machine on \((1^{\ell},s)\), with \(s\) binary, outputs integer lengths \(d,m\), and the evaluation machine on \((1^{\ell},s,z)\) writes the ordered list of all \(m\) sampled \(\ell\)-bit strings. Each runs in at most \(K(\ell+s+1)^q\) steps on valid inputs. Equivalently the time can be polynomial in \(\ell+m\), because of the polynomial relationship between \(s\) and \(m\). All preprocessing and output writing are counted. There is no advice, oracle, hard-function description or hard-function truth table available to these machines.

The constants and the machines precede the parameters, and \(H_{\ell,s}\) precedes the universal quantifier over \(f\). cards.title: Seeded extraction with constant total entropy loss
cards.formal:
Do there exist an explicit family of ordinary seeded extractors and absolute constants \(C,\Delta\in\mathbb N\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge2\) and \(0\le k\le n\), the family supplies a function
\[\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}:\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{d(n,k)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{m(n,k)}\]
with
\[d(n,k)\le C\lceil\log_2 n\rceil,\qquad 0\le k+d(n,k)-m(n,k)\le\Delta,\]
and, for every distribution \(X\) on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) with min-entropy at least \(k\),
\[\operatorname{TV}\bigl(\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}(X,U_{d(n,k)}),U_{m(n,k)}\bigr)\le1/100?\]
The seed is uniform and independent of \(X\). Explicitness means uniform deterministic evaluation in time polynomial in \(n\), with the same algorithm and polynomial for all \(n,k\). This is the constant-total-entropy-loss question in Vadhan's Open Problem 6.41.
cards.why: This asks whether an efficient general randomness purifier can preserve all but a constant number of the available random bits while using only a logarithmic seed. In applications that enumerate seeds or pay exponentially for entropy loss, the additive loss determines a multiplicative cost. Resolving the question would distinguish information-theoretic feasibility from the achievable efficiency of explicit extraction.

cards.definitions:
All lengths \(n,k,d,m\) are integers measured in bits, with \(d,m\ge0\), and logarithms have base two. For a finite random variable \(X\),
\[H_{\infty}(X)=-\log_2\max_x\Pr[X=x].\]
Thus the source promise is \(\Pr[X=x]\le2^{-k}\) for every \(n\)-bit string \(x\). The source may have arbitrary dependencies between its coordinates and need not be samplable by an efficient algorithm. The extractor receives a sample string, not a description of its distribution. \(U_t\) denotes the uniform distribution on all \(t\)-bit strings, including the unique empty string when \(t=0\). For distributions \(P,Q\) on the same finite set,
\[\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|.\]
The condition is statistical and quantifies over every promised source, with no computational restriction on a test of the output.

A family is explicit if there are two fixed deterministic multitape Turing machines and integers \(K,q\ge1\): a parameter machine on \((1^n,k)\), with \(k\) in binary, outputs \(d(n,k),m(n,k)\) in binary; an evaluation machine on \((1^n,k,x,y)\) outputs the entire \(m(n,k)\)-bit string. Both halt within \(K(n+1)^q\) steps on all valid inputs. All preprocessing and output writing are counted. There is no advice, oracle, randomized construction or length-dependent table supplied for free. The machines, \(C,\Delta,K,q\) are chosen before \(n,k\) and before the source distribution.

Total entropy loss means \(k+d-m\): it counts the source's guaranteed entropy together with all perfect seed bits consumed. This ordinary extractor requirement concerns the output distribution alone. It does not require that the output remain uniform when the seed is separately disclosed. A strong extractor, whose output is uniform jointly with a disclosed seed, may be converted to an ordinary one by including its seed in the total output, but those seed bits must then be counted in \(m\). The convention \(m\le k+d\) is harmless output truncation for this error level. Integer entropy thresholds suffice for the stated additive-constant target; rounding down a real threshold changes the loss by less than one bit.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed uniform construction claim. A positive answer must specify the algorithms and universal constants and prove the extraction guarantee, logarithmic seed bound, constant total loss and polynomial evaluation time throughout the parameter domain. A negative answer must rule out every such uniform family. An existence proof without efficient evaluation, a loss growing with \(n\) or \(k\), or an output bound that ignores consumed seed entropy does not meet the criterion.

cards.title: Extraction with log n plus constant seed length
cards.formal:
Is there an explicit family of ordinary seeded extractors with error at most \(1/100\), a rational constant \(\gamma\in(0,1]\) and an integer constant \(C\ge0\) such that, for all integers \(n\ge2\) and \(0\le k\le n\),
\[\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}:\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{d(n,k)}\to\{0,1\}^{m(n,k)},\qquad d(n,k)\le\lceil\log_2 n\rceil+C,\qquad m(n,k)\ge\lfloor\gamma k\rfloor?\]
For every distribution \(X\) on \(n\)-bit strings satisfying \(H_{\infty}(X)\ge k\), and a uniform seed independent of \(X\), the required guarantee is
\[\operatorname{TV}\bigl(\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}(X,U_{d(n,k)}),U_{m(n,k)}\bigr)\le1/100.\]
The family, \(C\), \(\gamma\) and its polynomial evaluation bound must be uniform across \(n,k\). This selects the main \(m=\Omega(k)\) target in Vadhan's Open Problem 6.42, retaining its weaker polynomial-output alternative as context.
cards.why: A logarithmic seed is often enumerated over all possibilities. Fixing its leading coefficient at one makes that enumeration linear in the source length up to a constant factor, instead of an unspecified polynomial. Achieving substantial output at that seed length for arbitrary min-entropy would sharpen a central resource bound in explicit randomness extraction.

cards.title: Universal determinant evaluations for bipartite matching
cards.formal:
Can one construct, in uniform deterministic NC, an integer table
\[\alpha^{(m)}=(\alpha_{i,j}^{(m)})_{i,j\in[m]}\in\{0,1,\ldots,m2^{m^2}\}^{m^2}\]
for each integer \(m\ge1\), such that the same table works for every simple bipartite graph \(G\) with labeled vertex classes \([m]\) and \([m]\)? Precisely, define the integer matrix
\[A_G(\alpha)_{i,j}=\begin{cases}\alpha_{i,j}&\text{if }(i,j)\in E(G),\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\]
The requirement is
\[\forall G,\qquad \det A_G(\alpha^{(m)})\ne0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G\text{ has a perfect matching}.\]
The construction receives only \(1^m\), not \(G\). This card selects the NC construction explicitly proposed in Vadhan's Open Problem 3.7; its more permissive request for an efficient or even subexponential sequential construction is not an equivalent target.
cards.why: A universal evaluation table would give a reusable deterministic replacement for all random entries in the classical determinant test for bipartite matching. The same polynomial-size data would preserve every matching-existence test at a given graph size. The source uses NC construction as a particularly strong form of explicitness, connecting this algebraic derandomization object to efficient parallel computation.

cards.definitions:
The notation \([m]\) means \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\). A simple bipartite graph in the statement is an arbitrary subset \(E\subseteq[m]\times[m]\), with no multiple edges. A perfect matching is a permutation \(\pi\) of \([m]\) for which \((i,\pi(i))\in E\) for all \(i\). The determinant is over the integers:
\[\det B=\sum_{\pi\in S_m}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{i=1}^{m}B_{i,\pi(i)},\]
where \(S_m\) is the set of all permutations and \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\) is their parity sign. Nonzero means exact integer nonzero, not a floating-point test or a residue modulo an unspecified prime.

Encode each entry of \(\alpha^{(m)}\) as a nonnegative binary integer padded to
\[L_m=\lceil\log_2(m2^{m^2}+1)\rceil\]
bits, and list entries in row-major order. The output contains exactly \(m^2L_m\) bits. Exponentially large entry values thus have polynomially many bits; their entire encoding is counted.

Uniform deterministic NC here means a logspace-uniform Boolean circuit family computing this full output from \(1^m\). There are fixed positive integers \(K,a,b\) such that the circuit for length \(m\) has at most \(K(m+1)^a\) gates and depth at most \(K\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil^b\). Gates are fan-in-two AND and OR, unary NOT, input bits and Boolean constants. A single deterministic Turing machine, on \(1^m\), writes the circuit and its output-wire list using \(O(\log(m+1))\) work space and polynomial time. Its output tape is write-only and is not free readable memory. No random bits, advice, oracle or table depending on \(m\) is supplied. The constants, circuit-generation machine and computation family precede the universal quantifiers over \(m,G\). Arbitrary unit-cost operations on integers are not part of this Boolean model.

The graph can be represented by its \(m^2\)-bit incidence table when stating correctness, but it is not an input to the constructor. An assignment chosen separately for each graph, or an algorithm deciding matching using another matrix, does not by itself provide a universal scalar table in the specified range.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of this NC construction claim. A positive proof must specify the uniform circuit construction, its polynomial-size and polylogarithmic-depth bounds, the entry range, and the determinant equivalence simultaneously for every graph. A negative proof must rule out every such uniform NC family. Nonconstructive existence of the tables, graph-dependent substitutions, or an NC matching algorithm without the required universal tables is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The determinant polynomial of the symbolic bipartite adjacency matrix is nonzero exactly when a perfect matching exists. Distinct perfect matchings contribute distinct monomials before evaluation; cancellation between their evaluated integer contributions is the obstacle the table must avoid.

The source proves that a suitable table exists for each \(m\). There are \(2^{m^2}\) graphs, and a uniformly chosen table from the specified range makes the determinant vanish incorrectly for any fixed matching-containing graph with probability at most \(m/(m2^{m^2}+1)\). The resulting simultaneous-existence bound does not supply an efficient uniform constructor.

The 2016 Fenner–Gurjar–Thierauf result gives uniform circuits of quasipolynomial size and polylogarithmic depth for bipartite perfect matching. Quasipolynomial size exceeds the polynomial-size NC requirement in this card.

The July 2026 Chatterjee–Ghosh–Gurjar–Raj–Thierauf preprint claims NC algorithms for bipartite matching, including weighted and search versions. Its decision algorithm tests the rank of a larger block matrix built from the input graph. The checked construction is a different algebraic test and does not supply one scalar substitution into the original adjacency matrix for all graphs. This card therefore retains the universal-table question, while recording that its historical algorithmic motivation has a separate new claimed resolution.

cards.definitions: All languages and promise inputs are binary strings. A promise problem is a pair \((Y,N)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\); only inputs in \(Y\cup N\) require a correct answer. It is in \(\mathrm{prBPP}\) if a uniform randomized multitape Turing machine halts in \(C(n+1)^a\) steps on every input of length \(n\) and every random tape, for constants \(C,a\) depending on the machine, accepts every input in \(Y\) with probability at least \(2/3\), and accepts every input in \(N\) with probability at most \(1/3\). Random bits are independent and fair. The class \(\mathrm{prP}\) has the same total polynomial clock and promise requirement with a deterministic machine and exact correctness. The hypothesis quantifies over all promise pairs, with a potentially different deterministic machine and polynomial for each pair; it does not require a single effective transformation of programs. There is no correctness requirement off the promise. Define \(\mathrm{EXP}=\bigcup_{a\ge1}\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^a})\), with standard constant-factor time bounds, and \(\mathrm E=\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{O(n)})\). A Boolean circuit has \(n\) input bits, fan-in-two AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, constants, unrestricted fan-out and one output bit. Its size is its number of non-input gates, including constant gates. Let \(s_L(n)\) be the minimum circuit size computing the characteristic function of \(L\) on every length-\(n\) input. A language belongs to \(\mathrm{P/poly}\) when \(s_L(n)\le C(n+1)^k\) for all \(n\), for some constants \(C,k\); its circuits need not be generated uniformly. Thus the conclusion requires one fixed language \(L\in\mathrm{EXP}\) such that, for every integers \(k\ge1\), \(C\ge1\) and \(N_0\ge1\), some \(n\ge N_0\) satisfies \(s_L(n)>C(n+1)^k\). Hardness at infinitely many lengths is sufficient; hardness at all sufficiently large lengths is not part of the target.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated implication or its logical negation, using these promise, uniformity and circuit-size definitions. A negative answer must establish \(\mathrm{prBPP}=\mathrm{prP}\) together with \(\mathrm{EXP}\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\); a relativized counterexample only proves a relativization limitation. A lower bound in a nondeterministic class, a different hard language for each polynomial exponent, or a theorem with an additional unproved hypothesis does not establish the requested implication.

context_blocks.text: A promise separates the inputs on which an algorithm must answer correctly from those on which either answer is acceptable. This permits randomized decision procedures whose acceptance probability is guaranteed to avoid an intermediate interval only on valid inputs. The hypothesis derandomizes every such promise problem, and is stronger than merely identifying the classes of total decision languages.

Uniform algorithms use one finite program at every input length. A nonuniform circuit family may contain unrelated circuits at different lengths. The conclusion says that some language with a deterministic exponential-time algorithm still defeats every polynomial size bound in this more permissive computational model.

Vadhan states the question as Open Problem 8.8 for E and notes its equivalence to the EXP formulation. The distinction matters in stronger exponential lower bounds, but it does not change the polynomial-circuit separation requested here.

The surrounding source discussion records a consequence for NEXP, the nondeterministic exponential-time class. It also records a consequence giving, for each fixed circuit exponent, a hard language in NP. Neither statement supplies the single deterministic exponential-time language required by this card.

Lu, Oliveira, Ren and Santhanam still describe the necessity of nonuniform circuit hardness for derandomization as an open issue in their 2024 paper. Their Heavy Avoid results include uniform and infinitely-often characterizations; these have distinct quantifiers and do not assert the present implication.

A positive answer would show that fully eliminating bounded-error randomness necessarily entails a circuit lower bound at a deterministic exponential-time scale. This is a necessity question about derandomization: proving that some particular hardness assumption suffices for derandomization answers a different direction.

cards.title: Lossless condensers with constant output overhead
cards.formal:
Is there an explicit family of functions
\[\operatorname{Con}_{n,k}:\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{d(n,k)}\to\{0,1\}^{m(n,k)}\]
and absolute integer constants \(C,\Delta\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge2\) and \(0\le k\le n\),
\[d(n,k)\le C\lceil\log_2 n\rceil,\qquad k+d(n,k)\le m(n,k)\le k+d(n,k)+\Delta,\]
and for every distribution \(X\) on \(n\)-bit strings with \(H_{\infty}(X)\ge k\), there is a distribution \(Y_X\) on \(m(n,k)\)-bit strings satisfying
\[H_{\infty}(Y_X)\ge k+d(n,k),\qquad \operatorname{TV}\bigl(\operatorname{Con}_{n,k}(X,U_{d(n,k)}),Y_X\bigr)\le1/100?\]
The seed is uniform and independent of \(X\). The family must have one deterministic polynomial-time evaluator for all parameters. This is the lossless-condenser formulation of Vadhan's Open Problem 6.35, paired in the source with the expander question 5.36.
cards.why: A lossless condenser compresses an arbitrary weak source while preserving its available randomness. Constant output overhead would leave that randomness concentrated in a string only a constant number of bits longer than its entropy, using a short seed. In graph terms it asks for nearly collision-free expansion with an almost minimal number of right vertices, a useful resource in extraction and data structures.

cards.definitions:
All lengths are integers in bits and all logarithms have base two. The min-entropy of a finite distribution is \(H_{\infty}(X)=-\log_2\max_x\Pr[X=x]\). The input promise therefore says that every point has probability at most \(2^{-k}\). Input distributions may be arbitrary; their coordinates need not be independent, and they need not have efficient samplers. The input to the condenser is a sample string and a seed, not a distribution description. \(U_t\) is uniform on all \(t\)-bit strings, with the single empty string when \(t=0\). Statistical distance is
\[\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|.\]
The comparison distribution \(Y_X\) may depend on the entire source distribution. Its existence is a mathematical guarantee; no algorithm for producing or sampling it is required.

Explicitness means that two fixed deterministic multitape Turing machines compute the lengths from \((1^n,k)\) and the full output from \((1^n,k,x,y)\), respectively. The entropy parameter is binary, \(|x|=n\), and \(|y|=d(n,k)\). For some fixed positive integers \(K,q\), each computation uses at most \(K(n+1)^q\) transitions, including preprocessing and output writing. Lossless means that the comparison distribution preserves all \(k+d\) guaranteed input-and-seed entropy bits. The bounded quantity \(m-(k+d)\) is the output entropy gap, or output overhead, not lost entropy. The condenser is not required to output an almost-uniform string: it only has to be close to a distribution with the specified min-entropy. Uniformity conditional on a separately disclosed seed is not imposed.

There is an equivalent graph view for these parameters. Let \(N=2^n\), \(D=2^d\), \(M=2^m\), and \(K_0=2^k\). Treat the condenser as a neighbor function \([N]\times[D]\to[M]\), identifying integers with fixed-length binary strings. It defines a left-regular bipartite multigraph; seeds label edges, and repeated neighbors are permitted. The lossless condition is equivalent to requiring at least \((99/100)DK_0\) distinct neighbors for every set of exactly \(K_0\) left vertices. cards.definitions: A promise problem is a pair \((Y,N)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^{*}\); inputs outside \(Y\cup N\) have no correctness requirement. Membership in \(\mathrm{prNP}\) means that there are a fixed deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every \(x\in Y\), some \(u\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\) satisfies \(V(x,u)=1\), and for every \(x\in N\), every such \(u\) is rejected. Membership in \(\mathrm{prAM}\) means that there are a fixed deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(W\) and a polynomial \(q\) such that Arthur sends a uniformly random \(r\in\{0,1\}^{q(|x|)}\) to Merlin, who sees \(x,r\) and responds with \(u\in\{0,1\}^{q(|x|)}\); for \(x\in Y\), \(\Pr_r[\exists u:W(x,r,u)=1]\ge2/3\), and for \(x\in N\), this probability is at most \(1/3\). Merlin has no computational restriction. Equality means equality of the sets of promise problems recognized in these senses, with a potentially different verifier for each problem. A co-nondeterministic circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit \(C(r,u)\), using constants, fan-in-two AND and OR gates and unary NOT gates, with one output, ordinary input bits \(r\in\{0,1\}^a\), and universally quantified input bits \(u\in\{0,1\}^b\). Its size counts all input and internal gates; put \(m=\max\{2,\operatorname{size}(C)\}\), so \(a,b\le m\). Encode its gates in topological order, with binary predecessor indices and designated ordinary/universal inputs. For \(z\in\{0,1\}^m\), set \(D_C(z)=1\) exactly when \(C(z_1,\ldots,z_a,u)=1\) for every \(u\in\{0,1\}^b\); extra ordinary bits are ignored. Empty universal inputs mean one empty assignment. Define density \(\mu(C)=2^{-m}|\{z:D_C(z)=1\}|\). A targeted generator is one finite nondeterministic Turing machine \(H\), and constants \(K,d\), whose every branch on a valid description \(C\) halts in at most \(K(m+1)^d\) bit steps, either with a distinguished failure symbol or with an explicit nonempty finite list \(S\) of strings in \(\{0,1\}^m\). At least one branch must output a list on every \(C\). If \(\mu(C)\ge1/2\), then every branch that outputs a list must satisfy \(\exists z\in S:D_C(z)=1\). If \(\mu(C)<1/2\), no hitting property is required, but the branch and output-format requirements still apply. All descriptions, nondeterministic choices, list entries and output writes are charged. No random bits, oracle or advice is supplied. The machine can depend on its particular circuit input, not merely on circuit size. Explicit polynomial-length output lists are the table representation of the source’s generators with \(O(\log m)\) seed bits; no compact representation of an exponentially large list is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the equivalence or its logical negation under these definitions. The nontrivial unresolved implication is from promise-AM derandomization to the stated generator; the reverse implication is already established in the cited framework. A positive answer must obtain a single uniform generator with polynomial cost, at least one successful branch for every circuit and no incorrect successful branch on any dense circuit. A generator requiring advice, working only for infinitely many input lengths, using superpolynomial time or handling ordinary deterministic circuits alone does not establish the target. A relativized separation or a counterexample to one proposed generator does not by itself refute the unrelativized equivalence.

sentences: The question asks whether randomness can be removed from uniform shallow AND–OR computations using deterministic polynomial time.
Each randomized circuit must answer correctly with probability at least two thirds on every input.
A single polynomial-time procedure constructs the family’s circuit descriptions from the input length.
The deterministic simulator may use arbitrary polynomial-time computation and need not remain a constant-depth circuit.
Quasipolynomial simulation, correctness on most inputs and nonuniform deterministic circuits do not meet the full target.

cards.definitions: A Boolean function here is a total function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}\). A randomized circuit \(C_n(x,r)\) is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output, \(n\) data input bits \(x\), and \(m(n)\) random input bits \(r\). Input nodes may contain these bits, their negations, and constants zero and one. Internal nodes are unbounded-fan-in AND or OR gates. There are no parity, majority, threshold or oracle gates. The depth is the maximum number of internal gates on an input-to-output path, and the size is the number of internal gates. Repeated wires into one gate are omitted. The entire circuit is encoded by an explicit ordered list of nodes, labels and predecessor lists with binary indices. A family witnesses \(f\in\mathrm{BPAC}^0\) if there exist fixed positive integers \(a,b,d\), a constant \(K\ge1\), and one deterministic algorithm \(M\) such that, for every \(n\ge0\), \(M\) given \(1^n\) outputs the circuit \(C_n\) in at most \(K(n+2)^a\) Turing-machine steps; its depth is at most \(d\), and both its size and \(m(n)\) are at most \(K(n+2)^b\). On every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), independent fair random bits \(R\), uniform in \(\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\), satisfy \(\Pr[C_n(x,R)=f(x)]\ge2/3\). The constants, circuit-generation algorithm and random-bit bound may depend on the family but not on \(n\), \(x\) or the random choices. Polynomial-time uniformity is required; merely having a circuit at each length is insufficient. The class \(\mathrm P\) consists of the functions computed correctly on every binary input by one deterministic multitape Turing machine in at most \(K_0(n+2)^{b_0}\) worst-case steps, for some constants \(K_0,b_0\). That machine has no random bits, advice or oracle. It may depend on the randomized family, and its polynomial exponent need not be the same for all families. The target concerns class containment, with no additional demand for an algorithm that takes arbitrary family-generating programs and produces their deterministic simulators. The notation \(\mathrm{AC}^0\), used in the context below, means the analogous polynomial-time-uniform family with no random inputs.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0\subseteq\mathrm P\), or of its negation under the stated uniformity convention. A positive answer must give exact, all-input polynomial-time simulation for every such family. A negative answer requires a total function in uniform \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0\) with no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. Average-case correctness, quasipolynomial simulation, deterministic circuits without a uniform construction, or a failure to build one particular pseudorandom generator is insufficient. A proof of the stronger uniform equality \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0=\mathrm{AC}^0\) also answers the stated containment question, but preservation of constant depth is not required.

context_blocks.text: The randomized computation is shallow, but its random input can contain polynomially many bits. Trying every possible random string can therefore require far more than polynomial time. The desired simulator need only compute the same final bit; it is not required to retain the shallow circuit shape.

Uniformity is essential. A polynomial-time algorithm must be able to obtain the description for each length from that length alone. An existence theorem for a separately chosen circuit or separately chosen good random strings at every length does not provide such an algorithm.

Vadhan’s Definition 7.26 explicitly permits polynomial-time uniform construction. Open Problem 7.31 asks for the stronger equality \(\mathrm{BPAC}^0=\mathrm{AC}^0\), or at least containment in \(\mathrm P\). This card selects the latter, already stated alternative, matching its original polynomial-time title.

The source’s Corollary 7.30 gives a deterministic quasipolynomial-time simulation: time \(2^{(\log(n+2))^{O(1)}}\), with constants depending on the fixed family. It also records a quasipolynomial-size constant-depth simulation. Neither guarantee supplies polynomial time.

Shaltiel’s work gives uniform weak derandomization for constant-depth computations, where the deterministic result is correct on most inputs. It also notes that the nonuniform randomized and deterministic constant-depth classes coincide. Those statements leave this card’s simultaneous uniformity and all-input correctness requirement unresolved.

Lyu’s 2022 Theorem 1 constructs generators fooling depth-\(d\), size-\(S\) circuits within error \(\varepsilon\), with seed length \(O((\log S)^{d-1}\log(S/\varepsilon)\log\log S)\), for fixed \(d\) and \(S\) large enough. Here “fooling” means that every circuit’s acceptance probability changes by at most \(\varepsilon\). This is a substantial quantitative improvement, but its general fixed-depth seed bound is not \(O(\log S)\).

A pseudorandom generator is a useful comparison point, but its optimal construction is a separate, stronger-looking formulation. This question permits any deterministic simulator meeting the stated time and correctness requirements, without prescribing a generator or any other proof method.

cards.title: Universal traversal sequences under arbitrary labels
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A\) and absolute positive integers \(C,b\) such that, for every pair of integers \(n,d\ge1\), on input \((1^n,1^d)\) the algorithm outputs in at most \(C(n+d+2)^b\) steps a word \(w=w_1\cdots w_T\in[d]^T\), with \(T\le C(n+d+2)^b\), satisfying the following universal property? For every connected undirected \(d\)-regular port-labeled multigraph on \(n\) vertices in the convention below and every starting vertex \(s\), the walk that successively takes absolute port numbers \(w_1,\ldots,w_T\) visits all vertices.
cards.why: A universal traversal sequence replaces all random choices in a walk by one short deterministic instruction list, without inspecting the graph. Efficient construction under arbitrary local labels would expose how far randomness can be removed when a walker cannot use information about its incoming edge or leave memory on vertices.

sentences: A universal traversal sequence is one list of absolute local port numbers that visits every vertex of every graph of a specified size and degree.
The graph may have parallel edges and self-loops, and its local port labels are arbitrary.
The question asks for a deterministic polynomial-time constructor given only the size and degree parameters.
Short sequences are known to exist, but incoming-port-based exploration and polynomial cover time with expensive local computation are different guarantees.
An efficient construction would remove randomness from graph-independent traversal under severely restricted information.

cards.definitions:
Use \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). A port-labeled multigraph is specified mathematically by a map \(h:[n]\times[d]\to[n]\). The \(d\) ports at each vertex are distinct local labels; different ports may lead to the same neighbor. Undirectedness means \[ \forall u,v\in[n]:\quad |\{i:h(u,i)=v\}|=|\{j:h(v,j)=u\}|.\] This represents equal directed multiplicities in opposite directions. A self-loop is allowed and consumes one port, following the textbook’s directed-edge convention. A graph is connected when any two vertices are joined by a finite walk through its ports. No compatibility between the port numbers at opposite ends of an edge is imposed.

For a word \(w\) and start \(s\), define \(v_0=s\) and \(v_t=h(v_{t-1},w_t)\) for \(1\le t\le T\). Universality requires \(\{v_0,\ldots,v_T\}=[n]\). The same word must work for all maps \(h\) obeying those conditions and for every start. At step \(t\), the word specifies the absolute outgoing port \(w_t\), independently of the vertex, prior walk, or the port through which the walker arrived. There is no incoming-port-dependent offset, backtracking instruction, mutable vertex memory, or graph-dependent change to the word.

The constructor receives only the unary size and degree parameters, not \(h\), \(s\), a graph oracle, advice or a random seed. It is one finite deterministic multitape Turing program; all its work, preprocessing and output are counted. Each port number is output in binary with a delimiter, so writing the entire sequence is included in the polynomial time bound. The polynomial is in the values \(n,d\), not their binary encoding lengths. This card selects the polynomial-time construction explicitly offered in Open Problem 3.9; a logarithmic-workspace constructor is a stronger possible outcome, not an additional requirement. The target is exactly \(n\) vertices as in Example 3.8. For a parameter pair admitting no connected graph in this convention, the universal condition is vacuous.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that a uniform constructor with the stated polynomial bounds exists, including universality for every local labeling and every starting vertex, or prove that no such constructor exists. Nonconstructive existence of a short sequence is insufficient, as is a construction whose running time is superpolynomial. A universal exploration sequence whose next outgoing port depends on the incoming port is a different object and does not by itself meet this target. The negative answer concerns all such constructors, not the failure of one proposed sequence.

context_blocks.text: The textbook uses undirected multigraphs with arbitrary local port labels. Polynomial-length words visiting every vertex of every graph in a fixed size/degree class exist, as recorded in Example 3.8. The open issue is the efficient deterministic production of such words.

Open Problem 4.48 restates Open Problem 3.9. The earlier statement expressly permits polynomial-time construction as a target and also mentions the stronger logarithmic-space possibility. This card retains the first option and the full multigraph family; the complete-graph example in the later statement is not substituted for the general target.

The textbook records polynomial-length logspace constructions for a restricted consistent labeling convention, and quasipolynomial-length constructions for general labels. A consistently labeled graph there has no two distinct vertices with the same \(i\)-th neighbor for any fixed port \(i\). Arbitrary labels in this card do not satisfy that promise.

The 2025/2026 exploration paper carefully distinguishes absolute-port traversal sequences from universal exploration sequences that can use the incoming port. It also separates the number of moves from the time spent computing them: a nonconstructively chosen traversal word can have polynomial cover time even when its local computation is extremely expensive. Its newer algorithms may keep mutable memory on vertices. These model differences prevent their cover-time guarantees from answering the construction question here.

cards.definitions: A language is a subset of \(\{0,1\}^*\); \(U_n\) is uniform on length-\(n\) binary strings. BPP consists of languages decided by a uniform randomized Turing machine in polynomial worst-case time on every random tape, with error at most \(1/3\) on each input and independent fair coins. Each \(A_{L,k}\) is one deterministic Turing machine with no advice and a worst-case polynomial time bound; its code, exponent and sufficiently-large-length threshold may depend on \(L,k\). No joint polynomial dependence on \(k\) is required. The displayed error is an input fraction at every sufficiently large length, not a probability over simulation coins. NEXP consists of languages recognized by nondeterministic Turing machines in time \(2^{n^a}\) for some fixed integer \(a\ge1\), allowing constant factors and finitely many small lengths. P/poly consists of languages whose length-\(n\) characteristic functions have polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no uniformity between lengths. Boolean circuits are finite acyclic networks of fan-in-two AND and OR, unary NOT, input bits and constants, with one output. Circuit size is the length of an explicit binary gate-and-wire encoding. For \(m\ge1\), \(\operatorname{Perm}_m(X)=\sum_{\pi\in S_m}\prod_{i=1}^m X_{i,\pi(i)}\) is a formal polynomial in \(m^2\) indeterminates, where \(S_m\) is the set of permutations of \([m]\). Arithmetic circuits use fan-in-two addition, subtraction and multiplication, variable leaves and only the constants 0 and 1; there are no divisions or other field constants. They must compute the permanent as a formal polynomial over the integers, not merely on Boolean matrices. Polynomial size means one polynomial bound in \(m\) for all sufficiently large dimensions; the individual circuits need not be uniformly constructible. Thus a non-polynomial circuit conclusion excludes every fixed polynomial bound, rather than demanding an eventual exponential lower bound. The assertion is an ordinary logical implication, with no restriction to a black-box proof.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of this exact implication, or a Lean refutation establishing the heuristic premise together with polynomial-size circuits for every NEXP language and for the permanent in the stated arithmetic model. An unconditional proof of either circuit lower-bound conclusion suffices. A uniform time-class separation, a different simulation premise or an impossibility restricted to a chosen proof method does not settle the assertion.

cards.definitions:
The input \(1^{n}\) is unary: a string of \(n\) copies of the symbol 1. The output is the ordinary binary representation of an integer. An \(n\)-bit prime is an integer \(p\) in \([2^{n-1},2^{n})\) whose only positive divisors are 1 and \(p\). The domain begins at \(n=2\), since there is no one-bit prime.

The machine is a single classical probabilistic Turing machine, with independent unbiased random bits and a polynomial worst-case running-time bound on every random tape. There is no advice depending on \(n\), precomputed table of primes, oracle, or free preprocessing. All computation, including any primality tests, counts toward its time bound.

Pseudodeterminism means that for each fixed length there is one fixed prime \(p_{n}\) returned with the stated probability across independent executions. The prime may depend on the algorithm and on \(n\), but not on the execution’s random bits. It need not be the smallest \(n\)-bit prime or a prime prescribed in advance. The remaining probability mass may produce a failure symbol, another prime, or an invalid output.

The guarantee is required at every length. Success on infinitely many unbounded lengths alone does not suffice. A guarantee for all sufficiently large lengths would suffice, since finitely many shorter lengths can be handled by a fixed finite part of the algorithm.

The constant success probability is the usual bounded-error convention for pseudodeterminism. Independent repetitions followed by a majority output can amplify concentration on the same canonical prime with polynomial overhead. Merely finding some prime with high probability, while different runs usually return different primes, does not meet the requirement.

The source lists several distinct search tasks. This card explicitly selects prime generation as its main target; it does not assert that solving it is equivalent to making every randomized search problem pseudodeterministic.
